new.title: How Regex::new() works
new.description: Compiles a pattern once, so it can be used many times; a bad pattern is an error.

l1.text: \d = any digit,  + = one or more times

l4.text: a group is opened but never closed

slides.caption: Regex::new() reads the pattern text and builds a matcher from it. This is the slow part, so it is done once.
The pattern \d+ is parsed: \d means one digit, + means one or more of what comes before it.
The pattern is valid, so the compiled matcher comes back as Ok(Regex). Keep it and reuse it: searching with it is fast.
Now "(": a group is started, but there is no ")" to end it.
Regex::new() does not panic on a bad pattern; it returns Err with a message that points at the problem.
r"\d+" → Ok, "(" → Err. Write patterns as raw strings (r"...") so the backslashes reach the regex unchanged.

is-match.title: How Regex::is_match() works
is-match.description: Says whether the pattern matches anywhere in the text.

note.text: re = Regex::new(r"\d+"): one or more digits

slides.caption: is_match() looks for the pattern anywhere in the text. It only answers yes or no.
a, b and c are not digits, so no match starts there.
At 1 a digit is found, so the pattern matches. is_match() can stop right here: it does not need to know where the match ends.
The pattern matches anywhere in the text unless it is anchored: r"^\d+$" would need the whole text to be digits, and "abc123" would give false.
re.is_match("abc123") is true. Use find() when you also need where the match is.

find.title: How Regex::find() works
find.description: Gives the first, leftmost match and where it is.

slides.caption: find() returns the first match, as an Option<Match> with the matched text and its byte positions.
The search starts at the left. a and b are not digits.
At index 2 a digit starts a match. + is greedy: it takes as many digits as it can, so it takes 2 as well.
c is not a digit, so the match ends before index 4. The match is "12", from 2 up to (not including) 4.
find() stops after the first match. "345" is also a match, but it is not looked at.
find() returns Some(Match) with as_str() = "12", start() = 2 and end() = 4. Use find_iter() for every match.

find-iter.title: How Regex::find_iter() works
find-iter.description: Yields every match, left to right, without overlaps.

slides.caption: find_iter() repeats the search: after each match it continues from where that match ended.
The search goes on from index 4. c and d are skipped.
The next match is "345" at 6..9. Matches never overlap, because each search starts after the previous match.
The end of the text is reached, so the iterator ends.
Collected with .map(|m| m.as_str()), the matches are "12" and "345".

captures.title: How Regex::captures() works
captures.description: Finds a match and gives the parts matched by each group in ( ).

slides.caption: Each ( ) in the pattern is a capture group. captures() returns the whole match and what every group matched.
Group 1, the first (\d+), matches the digits 10.
The - in the pattern matches the - in the text. It is not inside a group, so it is not captured on its own.
Group 0 is always the whole match: "10-20".
caps[1] is "10" and caps[2] is "20" (indexing panics if a group did not match; caps.get(1) returns an Option).

captures-name.title: How Captures::name() works
captures-name.description: Gets a capture group by its name instead of its number.

slides.caption: (?P<year>...) gives a group a name. \d{4} means exactly 4 digits, \d{2} exactly 2.
The group named year matches the first 4 digits.
The - matches, then the group named month matches 2 digits.
caps.name("year") looks the group up by name and returns Some(Match). Names keep code readable when groups are added or moved.
caps.name("year") is Some("2024") and caps.name("month") is Some("03"). An unknown name gives None.

captures-iter.title: How Regex::captures_iter() works
captures-iter.description: Gives the capture groups of every match.

slides.caption: captures_iter() is find_iter() with groups: for each match it yields a Captures. \w+ is one or more letters, digits or _.
First match: group 1 is "a", group 2 is "1".
The space does not match, so the search moves on.
Second match: group 1 is "b", group 2 is "22".
Mapped with |c| (c[1].to_string(), c[2].to_string()), the matches give ("a", "1") and ("b", "22"). Parse the numbers with .parse() if you need integers.
replace() finds the first match and puts the replacement in its place.
The first match is the digit 1.
replace() stops after one replacement: the 2 is also a digit, but it stays.
replace() returns "a#b2" as a Cow<str>: if nothing matches, the original text is returned without copying. Use replace_all() for every match.

replace-all.title: How Regex::replace_all() works
replace-all.description: Replaces every match; $1, $2 insert the groups.

slides.caption: replace_all() replaces every match. In the replacement, $1 and $2 stand for what group 1 and group 2 matched.
The match "10-20" has group 1 = "10" and group 2 = "20".
There are no more matches, so the result is complete. With more matches, each would be swapped the same way.
replace_all("10-20", "$2-$1") gives "20-10". Write ${1}x when a letter follows a group number, or $1x is read as a group named 1x.

split.title: How Regex::split() works
split.description: Cuts the text at every match of the pattern.

note.text: re = Regex::new(r"[,;]"): a comma or a semicolon

slides.caption: split() uses the matches as separators and yields the text between them. [,;] matches one character that is , or ;.
The first separator is the comma. The text before it, "a", is yielded.
The next separator is the semicolon: "b" is yielded.
After the last separator comes "c". The separators themselves are not part of the result.
split() yields "a", "b", "c". str::split can only split on fixed text; a regex can split on several kinds of separators at once.

splitn.title: How Regex::splitn() works
splitn.description: Splits into at most n pieces; the last piece keeps the rest.

slides.caption: splitn(text, 2) splits like split(), but stops when it has 2 pieces.
The first comma splits off "a". That is piece 1.
Piece 2 is the last one allowed, so it is everything that is left, commas included.
The other commas are not used as separators.
splitn(.., 2) gives "a" and "b,c,d". Useful for "key=value=more" when only the first = separates the key.

escape.title: How regex::escape() works
escape.description: Makes text match literally by escaping the characters that have a meaning in patterns.

note.text: + means "one or more" in a pattern

slides.caption: In a pattern, + is an operator. To search for the text "1+1=2" itself, the + must be escaped.
escape() checks every character. 1 is a plain character: unchanged.
+ has a meaning in patterns, so a backslash is put in front of it: \+.
escape() returns "1\+1=2". Regex::new(&regex::escape(text)) matches exactly that text. Without escaping, "1+1=2" would match "11=2" or "111=2".

regex-set-matches.title: How RegexSet::matches() works
regex-set-matches.description: Tests many patterns against a text in one pass.

slides.caption: A RegexSet compiles several patterns together. matches() scans the text once and reports which patterns match somewhere.
Pattern 2, !, matches nowhere: there is no ! in "a1".
matches() returns a SetMatches holding the indices 0 and 1. It does not say where each match is; use the separate Regex for that.
set.matches("a1").into_iter() yields 0, 1. Handy for routing: one scan tells which of many rules apply.

as-str.title: How Regex::as_str works
as-str.description: The pattern text the regex was built from.

slides.caption: Useful in error messages and logs.

captures-len.title: How Regex::captures_len works
captures-len.description: How many groups the pattern has, counting the whole match as group 0.

slides.caption: Group 0 is always the whole match.

capture-names.title: How Regex::capture_names works
capture-names.description: The name of each group, None for unnamed ones.

slides.caption: One entry per group, in order. Group 0 (the whole match) never has a name.
Use the names with caps["y"] or caps.name("y").

static-captures-len.title: How Regex::static_captures_len works
static-captures-len.description: The number of groups that always take part in a match, if that is fixed.

slides.caption: An optional group makes the count variable: None.

shortest-match.title: How Regex::shortest_match works
shortest-match.description: Where the earliest match could end; faster than find when you only need yes and a position.

note.text: end of the first possible match

slides.caption: It stops as soon as a match is certain, so the end may be shorter than find() reports.

find-at.title: How Regex::find_at works
find-at.description: Like find, but starts searching at a byte offset.

slides.caption: find_at skips the text before start, but still sees it for anchors like \b.
The first digit from there is "2" at index 3.
Positions stay relative to the whole text, not to start.

is-match-at.title: How Regex::is_match_at works
is-match-at.description: Whether there is a match starting at or after a byte offset.

slides.caption: The "1" before the offset is not searched.

captures-at.title: How Regex::captures_at works
captures-at.description: Like captures, but starts at a byte offset.

slides.caption: Group positions stay relative to the whole text.

replacen.title: How Regex::replacen works
replacen.description: Replaces only the first n matches.

slides.caption: replacen stops after n replacements; n = 0 means replace all of them.
The third digit stays because the limit is 2.
Borrowed from the searched string, no copy.

match-start.title: How Match::start works
match-start.description: Byte offset where the match begins.

slides.caption: end() is one past the last byte.

match-end.title: How Match::end works
match-end.description: Byte offset just after the match.

match-range.title: How Match::range works
match-range.description: The byte range of the match.

match-len.title: How Match::len works
match-len.description: Length of the match in bytes.

slides.caption: x* can match nothing at position 0.
Patterns that can match nothing need care in loops.

captures-get.title: How Captures::get works
captures-get.description: The Match of a group by number, or None if that group did not take part.

slides.caption: get(0) is the whole match, get(1) the first group, and so on.
get(9): there is no group 9, so None (caps[9] would panic).
An optional group that did not match also gives None.

caps-iter.title: How Captures::iter works
caps-iter.description: Every group in order, as Option<Match>.

slides.caption: Unmatched optional groups appear as None.

captures-len-caps.title: How Captures::len works
captures-len-caps.description: The number of groups, including group 0.

captures-extract.title: How Captures::extract works
captures-extract.description: The whole match and a fixed-size array of group texts.

slides.caption: extract::<N>() gives &str values directly, which is handy with let-destructuring.
The two groups as an array.
It panics if N does not equal the number of groups.

captures-expand.title: How Captures::expand works
captures-expand.description: Fills a template like "$m/$y" with group texts.

slides.caption: $name or $1 refer to groups; ${y} avoids ambiguity.

builder-new.title: How RegexBuilder::new works
builder-new.description: Starts building a regex with options.

slides.caption: Set flags with the builder methods, then call build().

builder-case-insensitive.title: How RegexBuilder::case_insensitive works
builder-case-insensitive.description: Makes letters match regardless of case.

slides.caption: Same as writing (?i) in the pattern.
Unicode-aware: also for letters like É.

builder-multi-line.title: How RegexBuilder::multi_line works
builder-multi-line.description: Makes ^ and $ match at every line, not only at the ends of the text.

slides.caption: By default ^ is the start of the text. In multi-line mode it is the start of each line.
Useful for blocks of text across lines.

builder-ignore-whitespace.title: How RegexBuilder::ignore_whitespace works
builder-ignore-whitespace.description: Allows spaces and # comments inside the pattern.

slides.caption: Spaces are ignored; use \ or [ ] for a literal space.

builder-swap-greed.title: How RegexBuilder::swap_greed works
builder-swap-greed.description: Makes x* lazy and x*? greedy.

slides.caption: a+ now takes as little as possible.
Usually clearer to write a+? instead.

builder-unicode.title: How RegexBuilder::unicode works
builder-unicode.description: Turns Unicode-aware classes like \w on or off.

builder-size-limit.title: How RegexBuilder::size_limit works
builder-size-limit.description: Caps how big the compiled regex may get.

slides.caption: Large repetitions of Unicode classes compile to big machines.
Important when patterns come from users.

builder-build.title: How RegexBuilder::build works
builder-build.description: Compiles the pattern with the chosen options.

slides.caption: An unclosed group is an error.

set-new.title: How RegexSet::new works
set-new.description: Compiles several patterns to be matched in one pass.

slides.caption: A set answers which of its patterns match, scanning the text only once.
It tells you which patterns match, not where.

set-is-match.title: How RegexSet::is_match works
set-is-match.description: true if any pattern of the set matches.

set-len.title: How RegexSet::len works
set-len.description: How many patterns the set holds.

set-patterns.title: How RegexSet::patterns works
set-patterns.description: The pattern texts, in index order.

slides.caption: Use it to show which pattern matched.
The index of each matches SetMatches.

set-empty.title: How RegexSet::empty works
set-empty.description: A set with no patterns, which never matches.

slides.caption: A neutral value, e.g. when no filters are configured.
Index into the patterns given to RegexSet::new.

set-matches-matched-any.title: How SetMatches::matched_any works
set-matches-matched-any.description: true if at least one pattern matched.

slides.caption: Same as RegexSet::is_match, after the fact.

set-matches-iter.title: How SetMatches::iter works
set-matches-iter.description: The indices of the patterns that matched, ascending.

slides.caption: Pattern 1 needs only letters, so it fails here.

set-matches-len.title: How SetMatches::len works
set-matches-len.description: The number of patterns in the set (not the number that matched).

slides.caption: A common surprise: this is not the match count.

bytes-is-match.title: How regex::bytes::Regex::is_match works
bytes-is-match.description: Matches against bytes, which need not be valid UTF-8.

slides.caption: A &str regex would refuse invalid UTF-8; the bytes version does not care.
Use it on file contents or network data.

bytes-find.title: How regex::bytes::Regex::find works
bytes-find.description: The first match in bytes, as a bytes Match.

captures-get-match.title: How Captures::get_match works
captures-get-match.description: The overall match (group 0), which always exists.
